name: Post-Blockchain Tech
subject: blockchain
subjectTitle: Blockchain: A Skeptic's Guide to Trust Technologies

lesson.title: It Turns Out You Did Not Need the Chain
lesson.summary: Many technologies first pitched as blockchain applications, zero-knowledge proofs, verifiable credentials, and decentralized identifiers, work perfectly well without an actual blockchain underneath them.
lesson.body:
This chapter is where the skeptic's guide pays off. Zero-Knowledge Proof, Verifiable Credential, and Decentralized Identifier were all, in their early years, marketed and prototyped as blockchain applications. It is worth asking directly: did any of them actually require a blockchain to work, or did the blockchain hitch a ride because it was the fashionable infrastructure of the moment?

Look at each in turn. Zero-knowledge proofs are pure cryptography between a prover and a verifier. The foundational research dates back decades before blockchain existed, and the technique works identically whether or not a ledger is involved anywhere. Zcash uses zero-knowledge proofs on a blockchain, but a bank could use the same underlying math to let a customer prove solvency without disclosing an exact balance, with no chain required at all. Verifiable credentials need only a digital signature scheme and an agreed data format. An issuer's signing key does not need to live on a blockchain, and most production credential deployments today, mobile driver's licenses among them, verify signatures against keys published through ordinary PKI or a government registry, not an on-chain record. Decentralized identifiers make this clearest of all: did:web resolves through plain DNS and HTTPS, and did:key is derived from a public key with no lookup at all, both fully functional identifier methods that never touch a distributed ledger.

Why did the blockchain get bundled in originally? Partly because Decentralized Trust was the animating idea behind all of these technologies, and a blockchain was the most visible, well funded example of trust without a central authority available while these standards were being designed, making it a natural first backend to reach for, especially for the subset of identifier methods that do publish to a ledger so document updates stay globally auditable. But the core value, proving something is true without over-disclosing, controlling your own identifier, holding a portable signed credential, turns out to be separable from any particular ledger technology.

The lesson generalizes past this one batch of technologies. When evaluating any blockchain-powered product, it is worth separating the genuinely useful cryptographic or architectural idea from the specific implementation choice to put it on a chain, using the same reasoning developed in Alternative Technologies and When Not to Use Blockchain. Sometimes the chain is doing real work, providing a shared, censorship-resistant, globally auditable log that no single party controls. Often, as with much of the identity stack covered in this batch, the real work was already being done by the cryptography itself, and the blockchain was optional infrastructure, not a load-bearing requirement.
